After several attempts, my hands stopped trying to do everything at ____6____. I could watch the scarves without chasing each one separately.

She pointed through her workshop window. At low tide, mud separated the slipway from the channel. A completed boat could not float across it simply because a party had been ____3____. I had been thinking of the boat as a finished ____4____. Mae was thinking of a journey that included the harbour. The tide belonged in her plan even though she could not ____5____ it.

Some tasks could continue inside the workshop; others required a particular water level. Experience helped her use the waiting time rather than treat every ____6____ as a failure. None of this meant that she worked without ____7____. Her schedule acknowledged outside conditions.

The customer eventually moved the gathering to the following afternoon. The boat arrived, the guests took photographs and the delay became part of the ____8____. He had been planning an occasion, while she had been planning a safe launch. They had used the same word, delivery, for activities with different ____9____. Explaining the tide gave them a way to make a shared arrangement.

I returned with unexpected material. My report still described the craft, but its centre was now the relation between skill and ____10____. A skilled worker does not control every condition; she knows which ones must be respected. I had imagined expertise as the power to make obstacles ____11____. Mae showed me another version: knowing when to adapt, when to explain and when to wait. The finished boat looked effortless afloat. Behind it lay hours of work and a decision not to ____12____. Our teacher asked why I included the mud. I found a ____13____. Without it, completion alone seemed to make launching possible. The mud made the missing ____14____ visible. The tide had done no work at the bench, but it had still helped determine when the boat could ____15____.
